title: FIA Asia Pacific Congress to Bring Member Clubs Together in the Philippines to Advance Mobility and Motor Sport Across the Region
summary: Members news    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, will be hosted by the Automobile Association Philippines (AAP) in Boracay in the Philippines for its Asia Pacific Congress next week, bringing together FIA Member Clubs from across the region.  From 29 September to 1 October, 120 delegates from Member Clubs across Asia and the Pacific, will unite in Boracay for three days of collaboration, innovation and knowledge sharing. Throughout the week, attendees will discuss priorities to advance safe and sustainable mobility for road users and drive greater motor sport accessibility.  The Asia-Pacific region is one of the FIA's most diverse and dynamic, spanning some of the world's fastest-growing mobility markets and an expanding motor sport community. The Congress will provide Member Clubs with an opportunity to share expertise and develop practical solutions which respond to the specific needs of their members and communities.  Across mobility, discussions will focus on road safety, innovation, sustainable and accessible transport, tourism and the changing needs of road users, building on the FIA's work to support Clubs in delivering meaningful impact at a national and regional level.  Motor sport sessions will explore opportunities to increase participation, strengthen grassroots competition and create more accessible pathways into the sport, supporting the FIA's ambition to make motor sport more affordable and accessible around the world.  The programme will also showcase the work and innovation of FIA Member Clubs across Asia-Pacific, providing a platform to share successful initiatives which can be adapted and scaled across the region.   H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said:   "The Asia-Pacific region is central to the future of both mobility and motor sport, and our Member Clubs are at the heart of that progress.   From improving road safety and embracing innovation to creating new opportunities for people to participate in motor sport, our Clubs are delivering real impact for their communities.    "The FIA Asia Pacific Congress gives us an important opportunity to bring that expertise together, share ideas and strengthen collaboration across one of the most diverse and dynamic regions in our Federation.    "I thank our hosts the Automobile Association Philippines, and President Joe Ferreria, for welcoming the FIA family to Boracay and look forward to another productive Congress."    FIA Region II President and President of host club the Automobile Association Philippines, Augustus ‘Joe’ Ferreria said:   "The strength of this region comes from the diversity, knowledge and ambition of our Member Clubs. Bringing our community together in the Philippines gives us the opportunity to learn from one another, identify shared challenges and develop solutions that can support Clubs across the region.    "The Asia Pacific Congress is an important moment for us to build on the progress already being made and ensure our Clubs have the tools, knowledge and connections they need to continue growing.    "We are proud to welcome the FIA and our fellow Member Clubs from across Asia-Pacific to the Philippines.”   The Congress follows a period of significant activity for the FIA across the region.  The FIA has expanded its  Safe Mobility 4 All & 4 Life  programme into Asia-Pacific, supporting Member Clubs and authorities with training and practical tools to improve road safety, while initiatives including the  FIA Innovation Challenge  continue to showcase Club-led solutions which can be shared and scaled across the Federation.  Across motor sport, the region continues to play an important role at every level of competition, from grassroots participation and regional championships through to the FIA's major World Championships with Malaysia set to host the Bahrain Grand Prix in the days following the congress.  The FIA Member Club structure forms the backbone of the federation’s governance and operations, with each full Member Club holding voting rights across the FIA’s elections and regulatory decisions. Clubs are grouped into two primary categories, with some serving in both roles:   Mobility Clubs – provide mobility services and represent the interest of road users, with a focus on road safety, travel and tourism, consumer rights, and sustainable mobility  National Sporting Authorities (ASNs) – govern and develop motorsport at a national level, are responsible for sporting events, issuing licenses, and engagement across regulations   Within the FIA there are four Mobility Regions and 6 sport zones. The FIA Asia Pacific Congress will welcome Member Clubs from across the region. The global FIA Membership is comprised of 246 clubs across five continents, connecting over 80 million members.      -ENDS-      For media enquiries please contact:   Geri Sherwin, Director of Presidential and Mobility Communications:  gsherwin@fia.com   George Mitchell, Mobility Communications Officer:  gmitchell@fia.com        About the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.   Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.       FIA  FIA   Members 1MembersFIAFIA00 Tuesday, September 22, 2026 - 11:07am  Tuesday, September 22, 2026 - 11:07am

title: F1 - 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix - Thursday Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  Mattia BINOTTO (Audi), Ayao KOMATSU (Haas), Laurent MEKIES (Red Bull Racing)     Q: Laurent, if we could perhaps start with you and Isack Hadjar, who’s had a very good week. Not only is he back in the cockpit here in Baku, he has also got a new contract for 2027 as well. Let’s talk about the comeback first of all. What convinced you that Baku was the right place and the right time for him to get back behind the wheel?    Laurent MEKIES:  You know, we always follow a very simple principle. We wanted to get Isack back when he was 100%, and perhaps even more importantly than that, when we were sure that we would not be taking any risk for his future long-term recovery. So, this was not possible in Zandvoort, not possible in Monza and Madrid. He had his last scan on Sunday this week and we had him on the simulator on Monday, and we couldn’t get him out of the simulator on Monday night. So, we felt it was a good enough test and he’s fit, and so it’s good to have him back. We are pretty convinced that he’s going to be close to 100%.    Q: Alright, let’s throw it further forward now. That new contract, was it an easy decision for you?   LM:  Yes, it was really easy, really. I think we discussed it a few times here through the season. He has done a very, very strong first part of the year. First with his natural speed, then with the way he has integrated with the team. Very quickly in the early weeks, he moved to the UK. He was pretty much every other week with us in Milton Keynes. And then, not less importantly, the way he has progressed through the races. We have really seen him doing something a bit better pretty much every race weekend. Therefore, it was a very, very easy decision to make.    Q: He was quite amusing in the press conference yesterday because he couldn’t tell us whether or not he had a multi-year deal. He said he didn’t know. Can you shed any light on that for us?   LM:  Isack has been with Red Bull for a very long time, and that means that, yes, we have a very long-term contract with him as part of him being part of our junior programme, and we have activated our options to secure him for 2027.    Q: Final one from me. Can we talk about the performance of the car? Do you feel that you’re on an upward trend at the moment?   LM:  Let me put it this way. We had two strong weekends in Monza and in Madrid. Now, strong weekends mean you fight for the podium. I think we had five or six podiums in the last seven races, so that’s a positive. Does it mean that we have had, in any of the races, the fastest car? No. So, we are close. We always knew the last one to three tenths would be the most difficult to cancel from the best competition. There are four teams that pretty much are within these two or three tenths, so you can slide very quickly from competing for pole to being on the fourth row. So we think, yes, we are getting closer. Whether or not it’s going to be enough to get that last step that will give us the fastest car pace, for that we think we still have some work to do.    Q: Okay, Laurent, thanks for that. Ayao, if we could come to you now. We’re going to start by talking about drivers, or driver actually, Esteban in particular. He said yesterday, and I’m quoting him, “I’m definitely a free agent next year.” Is that the case? How do you see his future at Haas?   Ayao KOMATSU:  Yes, we haven’t made any decision yet. But like Laurent said, every driver has a, let’s say, a closing certain point in the year to decide on the option. It just means that we haven’t decided on that option yet, but that was quite a long time ago. So his situation hasn’t really changed. We still are trying to finalise what we’re going to do for next year.    Q: So with him, it’s still an option for him to be at the team?   AK:  Yes. Like I said, we haven’t made any decisions yet.    Q: Okay. Can we talk in more general terms then about that seat alongside Ollie Bearman? What kind of driver are you looking for? Does it have to be an experienced driver, or would you go for youth if the right driver was available?   AK:  Look, what we’re looking for in the drivers, first and foremost, the guy needs to have speed. The guy needs to be fast. That’s something, you know, that’s their talent. We cannot teach them speed, so he needs to be fast, but really needs to be a team player, work closely with the team. And especially for a small team like us, those two drivers, the integration into the team, how they motivate the team, how they drive the team, is very, very important. It’s got to be a personal character that is very important for us. But I think it’s the same for any teams, but especially for teams like us. We are a small team, so it’s very, very important.    Q: Ayao, you’ve been busy with the TPC car recently. Can you put a timescale on this? When do you expect to make an announcement as to what’s happening next year?   AK:  Soon, within the next couple of weeks. We’ve done all the evaluations, so we’re just waiting to summarise our findings, have a discussion internally, have a chat with Gene, and then we’ll take the final decision.    Q: Okay, thank you for that. Can we talk about the car now? You’ve introduced various upgrades over the last couple of races. How much of a step forward has it been?   AK:  The one we introduced in Monza was a really good step forward. But just to put it in context, I mean, we started the season very well, but the one we did in Montreal, yes, that upped the performance in certain areas, but didn’t deliver everything. And also, we later found out the direction really wasn’t the direction we should have gone for. So, we made some mistakes there. Then again, for teams like us, it took us a long, long time to put those mistakes right. So finally, in Monza, we proved our hypothesis, assumption, and the work we’ve done addressed the issues in the correct way. So, not only put downforce on the car, but put downforce on the car that drivers can exploit. So that was really, really pleasing, and I think gives lots of confidence to everyone in the team. Identify the problem, solve it. But of course, in the future we try not to make the same mistake and also try to put that performance on the car quicker. So just trying to accelerate that process, that’s a challenge for us.    Q: Ayao, thank you for that as well. And Mattia, thank you for waiting. Let’s come to you now, and why don’t we start by talking about drivers as well. Tell us about the jobs that you think Nico and Gabi have done for you this year. Are you very happy with what they’ve done?   Mattia BINOTTO:  Very happy, yes, I would think that’s the answer. So, you need then to analyse. It’s a different situation for both of them. You’ve got an experienced driver, Nico, more a junior driver with Gabi. Nico is consistently delivering. I think Nico, when he’s come to, especially on the Sunday, the race, the consistency, being robust, very little mistakes, exploiting always the potential of the car, scoring points wherever there is a necessity or an opportunity. And I think that’s Nico. And so far, he has delivered well. Whenever he had an opportunity, he exploited the maximum potential for our car. Gabi is being more junior. It’s a learning phase, so it’s more, I think, we need to look at him more in his development, the rate of development. And here again, I have to say I can see his confidence growing race after race. You can see that he is becoming faster and faster, having obviously more confidence himself. No big mistakes, maybe a couple, but that’s part, again, of his learning phase. But overall, he is consistent as well. He is exploiting certainly the potential of the car. He is very fast in quali, on the single lap, when it matters. So overall, I have to say that I’m pretty pleased. So happy with the line-up, compared to both of them. I think our situation is even simpler. We have no discussion what’s the plan for the next season. Our drivers were contracted, so we knew that it would have been no change. But on top of that, I think we are happy on the speed of them. So, we never announced really what would happen next year because there was no necessity. So, we have a line-up which is confirmed and on which we are happy with.    Q: What about your junior driver, Freddie Slater, runner-up in F3, going up to F2 next year? Is he going to take on more F1 duties in 2027?    MB: Or maybe even earlier.  So, certainly Freddie is part of our driver development programme. High potential, he’s doing well. Just finished second in the championship. He was leading the championship before the last weekend in Madrid. Now finishing second. I think we discussed that with him. It can be as well a great lesson learned. Sometimes it’s not that, and that will be forgotten very soon. More important what he will deliver in the future. F1 duties yes, because that’s part of the development plan. F1 seat in the future, that will depend on how strong he will continue developing. But when you’ve got a driver in your academy, somehow the plans are for him, sooner or later, to be in your F1 seat. So again, happy with him, the way he has progressed. If you look at his F3 season since the start, where maybe he was abusing a bit too much on the tyres, he has become more balanced, managing better, getting experience and finishing very strong this season.    Q: What about the car? Heavily upgraded here in Baku, I think 14 registered upgrades on the car. What did you learn in FP1? Is it doing everything you expected?   MB:  FP1, first we had one car on the old package, the other one on the new package. It has been more gathering data, collecting data, and now we are going through all the analysis. I don’t think there is a proper performance comparison which has been concluded yet. Yes, if you look at the first, let me say, impression of the data, the package is delivering as expected, which is good, which is our main focus, as a matter of fact, for the weekend. For us, upgrading, yes, it’s important for the performance, it’s important for our fight in the championship. But again, for us, what’s more important is to make sure that the team is developing in terms of methodologies and capacity. So, from being brave when it comes in terms of mindset, to the type of aero concepts we may deliver, on the lead times, engineering, production, manufacturing, we raised the challenge. We raised the challenge, I think, with the upgrade we have brought here. It doesn’t matter how much it will deliver in terms of lap time. I think what matters for us the most is having raised the challenge, having again pushed the system on whatever is mindset and lead times. And hopefully the correlation will be, that’s the conclusion now of the exercise, hopefully we’ll have a correlation which is right compared to the wind tunnel and the sim.    QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR     Q: (Craig Slater – Sky Sports) A question for Ayao. So just to summarise what you just said, you might yet continue with Esteban, that’s a possibility. Could you go as far as to say it would be your intention to continue with Ollie Bearman in the other seat? And is he experienced enough now, and also in what he contributes to car development, that it wouldn’t be a risk to put a young driver potentially in the other seat if he carried on?   AK:  No, look, driver combination is obviously a pretty complex topic. Yes, we’ve been happy with Ollie as well. Like I said, we are still finalising our internal discussion. I really can’t say anything more than that.    Q: (Ted Kravitz – Sky Sports UK) This one’s for Laurent about the Red Bull young driver programme. Do you and your colleagues in the Red Bull young driver programme feel that Nikola Tsolov could benefit from maybe another preparation year before Formula 1? And is that bearing in mind that there may not be an opening at Racing Bulls for him anyway?   LM:  Look, first, Nikola is doing a very, very strong season. He is leading the championship and we are very, very happy with the progress he’s been making, both on track and from what we see he’s doing with us in Milton Keynes at the simulator. We think we have time to make the decisions on what’s going to happen for him next year. In all cases, a bit like when we discussed earlier for Isack, we have a long-term view on Nikola. What matters to us is that we make sure that we put him in the right environment so that all his potential is coming out. So, potential seems very high and we will make the decision in a few months on what his programme is for next year. For now, we’ll let him concentrate on a rather busy weekend here with three races in Baku.    Q: (Niccolò Severini – Sky Sports Italy) A question for Ayao. You said that you need a fast driver. Is there a strong option to put in the car a rookie, like maybe Rafael Câmara or Leonardo Fornaroli?   AK:  Yes, that’s why we’ve tested them. If that wasn’t the option, why do we test? And then, to be fair, all the three drivers we tested in Portimão, and also Jack in the last weeks, they’ve done a very, very good job. So, I think we are in a very fortunate position to have such interest from very talented drivers. So, we have just got to analyse the result very carefully because it’s a TPC test. It’s very, very difficult to normalise the condition, changing wind, the track temperature, lap time changes quite a lot. So yeah, it’s a very, very important decision, obviously. And of course, we’re talking about the lives of those people. You know, for those guys Formula 1 is always a dream to achieve. So, we’ve got to make the right decision. So yeah, that’s why we’re taking time to just make sure we do it right.    Q: (Sergey Podosenov – News.ru) To the three speakers. Beyond the track itself, what’s your general impression of Baku as a host city and organisation, the hospitality and the way the event is run?    MB:  I can start myself. Obviously, it’s not the first year or the first season we are coming. It has always been very enjoyable. It’s a unique circuit for characteristics because it was the, let me say, the circuit, the city patterns and the very long straight, which is the longest straight in the F1 calendar. If you look as well at the past years, a lot may happen during the race here, so the outcome and the result of the race is never guaranteed. It is always a big unknown before the race weekend, which I think makes it exciting. And then the city is more and more organised. You can see it. There are great facilities, great hotels very close to the circuit. You can even walk into the paddock from the hotels, often for most of the people at least, and I think that’s enjoyable. So at least I can speak for myself. It’s one of the circuits I’m coming and I’m enjoying.  AK:  Yes, you know, which other circuit we run next to a UNESCO World Heritage site! It’s such a very unique challenge. And then, like Mattia said, combination of the very, very long straight and the low-speed sections, tight sections, and also, as you saw in FP1, track evolution is huge. So, our team has got a very unique challenge to balance those things, and then lots can happen in the race. So that’s really nice. And then I love the old city, you know, the part of the city inside the castle. That atmosphere is really, really unique. So, I think the whole team really enjoys coming here very much.  LM:  Echoing what Mattia and Ayao have said, really, it became a classic in these 10 years. Fantastic track, fantastic racing, great vibes in the city, and some good memories also for Red Bull with the win last year here with Max. So, I think we all love coming here and racing here, and it’s never a boring weekend.    Q: (Thomas Maher – PlanetF1.com) A question for Mattia and for Laurent, please. Just in terms of the upcoming engine regulations on the V8s, where are you at in terms of the general principles that have been agreed? What do you want to see from the upcoming regulations? How important is it that a hybrid element is retained? And in terms of a timeline, when do the manufacturers need to get clarity on what’s happening?   MB:  There is no clarity yet. So, we know that FIA is still elaborating what may be the concepts they would like to propose. We know it’s a V8 for certain, 2030 the earliest introduction. On the timing, as you said, if it would be 2030, what does it mean in terms of starting the development? It has to be very soon. It has to be before the end of the year. I think the regulation needs to be agreed and voted before the end of the year to have certain clarities, by 2027, to start really the design and concept phase. What’s the main objective we are looking at? I think we all agree, first will be a significant cost saving required. The current power unit is still very expensive and we believe that having a clear target on cost would be important. When considering the format of the V8 itself, we believe that we still need to retain some advanced technologies. I think that F1 has always been the edge of the platform for innovation, ahead of technology, and we believe whatever will be the overall format, it has to remain a platform for innovation for all the manufacturers. So yes, welcome the V8, welcome a better sound, welcome a cost saving. And when it comes into the details of hybrid, I would say yes, turbo, possibly yes. But all the details, I think, need to be discussed with the FIA. That’s why I think that discussion will start very soon. As Audi, we are very open, very collaborative, and I’m pretty sure that together with the FIA we will find the right compromise.  LM:  Very similar here, honestly. Even though it’s a massive topic because, in the end, it will dictate the next generation of regulations. I think we are at the point where all the manufacturers, I don’t think we have very different ideas or very opposite ideas about what we all want from it. I think we want flat-out racing, flat-out qualifying. That will probably dictate the next architecture. And as Mattia said, you want flat-out racing, flat-out qualifying and retaining the technological challenge and the technological laboratories. And of course, we would like to do that also by ticking a few of the boxes. But I think in terms of these high-level objectives, with the FIA, with F1, with the teams, I think we are all pretty aligned. And how do you do it in the details, with the various options we have, it will be the discussion over the next few months. But in terms of what we want to achieve as stakeholders of the sport, I think we are all quite aligned.    Q: (Dzhastina Golopolosova – F1Maximaal.nl) My question to Laurent. Do you expect the ADUO situation will improve if next year they switch to 58/42?   LM:  Look, in terms of wanting to evolve the ADUO regulations, I think we can probably agree that the regulations were not exactly perfect and we will certainly welcome a discussion on making them evolve. I’m sure that sooner or later we’ll have these discussions with the FIA and the PU manufacturers. In the meantime, we have tried to make our point quite clear about where we think we can agree and where we think we don’t agree. And at some stage, we need to concentrate on ourselves and do the best job possible with the regulations we have.    Q: Mattia, is there anything you’d like to add with regards to ADUO?   MB:  No, I think Laurent mentioned it and I think it has been already past discussion. The current system, first, the regulation has been put in place for a safety net for the manufacturers which were clearly behind and had to catch up, or not to be staying frozen in a difficult situation for five seasons. The second was to support convergence, and this is what the main two concepts of regulations. So, safety net and convergence. If you look at how these things have developed, as I think Laurent mentioned, it’s not ideal yet. Fine-tunings are required. You may be trapped in a situation where maybe a top team got opportunity of development, while that cannot be safety net or convergence at the end. So how to develop a better regulation, I think, is exactly the discussion we need to have with the FIA. The ADUO concept is still valid. The fine-tuning is required.    Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) It’s another power unit question to Mattia and Laurent, please. Fernando Alonso said yesterday he still has hopes for some further tweaks for 2027, and he did one suggestion that Max Verstappen said he supports, which would be maybe to limit the peak power of the battery for longer to get more natural speed traces and not get your top speed halfway through the straight, but more towards the braking zone. Would you guys be open to any further tweaks, or do you feel the roadmap for ’27 and ’28 is fully set in stone?   LM:  So, the roadmap is a clear step forward compared to where we are here, with a rather small step next year and a significant step for 2028. As Oracle Red Bull Racing, we will support further tweaks if there is an agreement to further tweaks in the directions of flat-out qualifying, flat-out racing, which I think is what Fernando and Max were probably mentioning. Yes, we will support.  MB:  Obviously, what Fernando or Max said, I don’t know, needs to be evaluated. I think the concept certainly is to try always to improve the regulation. For ’27, already a significant change will happen, and I think first we need to go through that change and see what will be the result of the changes we’ve made in terms of flat-out racing, etcetera. So, I would be patient. I would wait to see first how much the changes we have, which are somehow significant, how much those changes will improve the situation, to furthermore, let me say, modify. And again, as Laurent said, we are always open for constructive discussions if further tuning would be required. It can be an idea, certainly open to it.    Q: (Adam Cooper – Adam Cooper F1) One for all three of you. At the moment, the last two races are going ahead as originally scheduled. Obviously Imola is on standby. Realistically, how long can you as teams wait for a decision? And if we are going to Imola, what sort of challenges will it present in the next couple of months? Ayao, why don’t we start with you?   AK:  Yes, I believe that Stefano was targeting to tell us in mid-October, right? So, we all know what the situation is. I believe that Imola is getting ready in case we have to do it. I think the challenges are, for instance, things like European motorhome structure, etcetera. All those people who look after them, they have a winter job, so we need to find alternative people to do that. But I’m sure we all, as a family, community, will make sure if we have to do that, that will happen. But hopefully, as a baseline, we can go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. That would be really good.  MB:  I don’t think there is much. As we discussed during the F1 Commission last Monday, mid-October is the last call for such a decision. The main challenges are more organisation and logistics. I would think, from a technical point, often we may say wintertime, snow tyres, but at the end, as a matter of fact, the average temperature in Imola in that time of the year is hotter than Las Vegas by the time we’ve got the race in Las Vegas. So I don’t think that’s a true concern. It’s more from the organisation and the logistics, really. And again, mid-October, hopefully we may do the right decision.    Q: (Ben Vinel – Motorsport.com) Question to Laurent. It has been nearly 10 years since anyone consistently matched Max’s performance as a teammate, and obviously he has become even stronger now. So, what do you expect from Isack for his second season at Red Bull? To be a decent second driver or to consistently challenge Max?   LM:  What we expect him to do is to continue to progress. So, what we have seen in that first part of the season, him improving his speed, not only the technical feedback, not only the maturity, not only the integration, improving his speed as he has been doing in the first part of the season. That’s what we would like him to continue doing through the second part of the year and through next year. If he does that, yes, of course he’s going to be very close to Max. So, both these things go together.    Q: (Nigel Chiu – Sky Sports) Laurent, there are quite a few upgrades on the Red Bull car this weekend. Is that the last major upgrade package for this season? How much focus is now going into next year’s car?   LM:  Yes, you’re right. It’s most probably our last significant package. We have switched a significant part of our resources, a very large majority of our resources, on next year’s car now. It doesn’t mean that we don’t look at this season. At first, we are still chasing our first win. That’s an important target for the team. And second, as you know, the regulations have only very little changes for next year and there are huge opportunities for us to continue to learn in the remaining races and to make sure we arrive as prepared as we can for next year. But in short, yes, it’s the last significant upgrade for this year.    Q: (Josh Suttill – The Race) Question for Mattia and for Laurent. On the topic of the next engine cycle, how important would it be to have some kind of push-to-pass system? Is that something on the agenda and something you’d advocate for?   MB:  Yes, it is on the menu. Push-to-pass is important for the racing situation, overtaking, so making sure that at least we are not creating trains and no one can overtake. So, a push-to-pass will be there. What’s the type of push-to-pass? Still to be discussed and agreed. So, there is not a clear, let me say, at the moment, way of doing it. There are multiple ways of doing it. It can be boost pressure, it can be DRS, it can be KERS, so electrical. So, the way to do it will be part of the discussions we will have with FIA.  LM:  Nothing to add to what Mattia said. It’s early days, but the intention is certainly to have great racing, to continue to have great racing.    ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Thursday, September 24, 2026 - 4:00pm  Thursday, September 24, 2026 - 4:00pm

title: F1 – Russell continues to set the pace in Baku as Antonelli recovers but Lindblad brings out red flags
summary: Sport news George Russell completed a Friday clean sweep at the Baku City Circuit as he set the pace in Free Practice 2 for the 2026 FIA Formula One Azerbaijan Grand Prix, leading Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli in a session disrupted by a red flag for Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad.  Russell’s best lap of 1:43.347s put him 0.552s clear of Antonelli, who had been forced to sit out much of the session after Mercedes changed his engine following the hydraulic issue that halted his FP1 running. Max Verstappen was third for Red Bull, 0.827s off Russell, with Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton completing the top five.  The session began with several drivers heading out on Medium tyres, while Antonelli remained in the garage as work continued on his Mercedes. Isack Hadjar had also required a gearbox change after FP1, while McLaren made further repairs to its cars, with temporary fixes visible on the floor assemblies.  Franco Colapinto had an unusual start to proceedings, heading into the Turn 2 run-off almost immediately after leaving the pit lane. Once the opening laps settled down, Russell moved to the top with a 1:46.300s before Verstappen went faster with a 1:45.933s.  Lando Norris then took over at the front with a 1:45.184s, despite running the Hard compound, but Verstappen responded immediately on the Mediums to reclaim P1 by 0.069s. The Dutchman was nevertheless unhappy with the balance of his Red Bull, reporting that he was “constantly counter-steering” as the rear axle lifted off the ground.   Russell then found more time, setting a 1:44.537s, only for Verstappen to respond by 0.045s. With the field pushing harder, the unforgiving nature of Baku soon made itself apparent. Lance Stroll brushed the wall at Turn 15, while Liam Lawson had a close moment at Turn 2 and Hadjar locked up heavily at Turn 1.  The first major interruption came when Lindblad carried too much speed through the tight Turn 8 section. The Racing Bulls driver clipped the barrier and made further contact on the uphill exit, bringing out the red flags. Lindblad emerged from the car unhurt but had completed only four laps by the end of the session.  Running resumed with just over half an hour remaining, allowing Antonelli to finally make his first appearance on track. His Mercedes team-mate continued to set the benchmark, however, lowering his time to 1:43.759s before improving again to 1:43.347s, helped by a slipstream from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto.  Leclerc briefly moved Ferrari to the top with a 1:44.473s before Russell reclaimed the position. Antonelli subsequently climbed to second, while Verstappen settled into third ahead of the two Ferraris. Hamilton ended the session fifth, followed by Norris, Pierre Gasly and Oscar Piastri.  The Soft-tyre runs gradually gave way to longer race simulations, with several drivers opting to continue their race preparation on the softer compound. The behaviour of the tyres suggested they could remain usable for extended runs around Baku, potentially making the harder compound less attractive for the race.  There were still several late incidents. Esteban Ocon ran into the Turn 15 escape road, while Norris made light contact with the wall at Turn 16 as he sought to maximise the exit.  At the chequered flag, Russell had completed 23 laps to finish 0.552s ahead of Antonelli, with Verstappen third and Leclerc fourth. Hamilton was fifth, ahead of Norris and Gasly, while Piastri and Hadjar completed the top nine.  After topping both Friday sessions, Russell heads into Saturday with Mercedes having established an early benchmark. title: F1 – Russell tops FP1 in Baku ahead of Verstappen as hydraulic issue sidelines Antonelli
summary: Sport news George Russell set the pace in a disrupted opening Free Practice session for the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship Azerbaijan Grand Prix, with the Mercedes driver edging Red Bull’s Max Verstappen by 0.4s around the Baku City Circuit.  Championship leader Kimi Antonelli had earlier set the benchmark but saw his session cut short when he stopped at Turn 7 after reporting a hydraulic problem. The Mercedes driver completed just nine laps, bringing out the Virtual Safety Car as marshals attended to his stricken car.  With the streets largely green at the start of the session, several drivers headed out early to help clean the racing line. Red Bull Racing’s Arvid Lindblad was among the first on track, running aero rakes as part of his programme alongside team-mate Liam Lawson.  Grip was initially at a premium, with Isack Hadjar, back in the Red Bull Racing car after recovering from a wrist injury, reporting difficulty under braking and admitting he had nearly hit the wall. McLaren’s Oscar Piastri also complained of significant brake vibration, while Verstappen later reported that his Red Bull was pulling to the right even when travelling in a straight line.  Charles Leclerc set the early benchmark with a 1:54.395, but lap times quickly tumbled as the track improved. Verstappen moved into the lead with a 1:49.202 before Leclerc responded with a 1:49.025. The Red Bull driver continued to find time, eventually setting a 1:46.512, although several drivers struggled to keep their cars under control over the bumpy surface.  Antonelli then moved to the top of the order with a 1:46.265, ahead of Lewis Hamilton, Verstappen, George Russell and Leclerc. However, the Italian’s session was soon brought to an abrupt end when he stopped at Turn 7 after reporting a loss of hydraulics. The Mercedes came to rest on track and a Virtual Safety Car was deployed while marshals attended to the car.  Once the circuit returned to green-flag conditions, Russell switched to the Soft tyres in an attempt to recover some of the running lost by Mercedes. The Briton survived a lock-up at Turn 3 but subsequently delivered a 1:45.387 thanks to a strong tow from Aston Martin’s Fernando Alonso to take the top spot.   Verstappen also encountered trouble on his first Soft-tyre run, locking up at Turn 1 before abandoning the lap. He later completed a clean run to go second with a 1:45.787, 0.400 seconds behind Russell. Leclerc was just 0.004s further back in third, with Hamilton fourth on a 1:45.824.  The opening session was less straightforward for McLaren. Piastri was instructed to return to the pits for a check, with the team investigating damage to the car. He subsequently remained in the garage for much of the session, although he was able to return later and eventually set a 1:46.398 for sixth.  Norris, meanwhile, completed only 14 laps after the team identified movement in the floor area of his McLaren. A temporary repair allowed the reigning champion to return to the circuit, but he finished 14th with a 1:46.981.  There were further interruptions elsewhere. Hadjar was forced to return to the pits with an engine-related problem after being instructed to remain in second gear, limiting him to just eight laps and leaving him 20th. Williams also experienced a brake issue, with Carlos Sainz suffering a fire in the pit lane before returning to action.  Lindblad briefly became stuck at Turn 7, while Hülkenberg stopped at Turn 4 and exited his Audi to help push it clear. Esteban Ocon subsequently stopped at pit exit.  Russell therefore ended FP1 fastest, with Verstappen, Leclerc and Hamilton all within 0.437s of the Mercedes. Antonelli’s early benchmark was good enough for fifth despite completing only nine laps, while Piastri, Lawson, Lindblad, Ocon and Gabriel Bortoleto completed the top 10. title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem meets with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev as Baku Celebrates a Decade of Racing
summary: FIA news His Excellency Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), met with His Excellency Ilham Aliyev, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, in Baku today to discuss shared priorities across motorsport and mobility.  The meeting, which took place during the Baku Grand Prix as the city celebrated a decade of racing on its iconic streets, provided an opportunity to discuss Azerbaijan’s continued development as a major international sporting destination, its established position within global motorsport, and opportunities to strengthen cooperation between the country and the FIA.  Azerbaijan has become an important destination on the international sporting calendar, with Baku providing one of Formula 1’s most distinctive city-centre settings and attracting fans and visitors from around the world.  The Presidents also discussed the wider role of mobility in supporting economic growth and connectivity, as well as the importance of road safety and sustainable transport as Azerbaijan continues to invest in its infrastructure and international connectivity.   FIA President, H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:   “It was a pleasure to meet with His Excellency President Ilham Aliyev and discuss our shared ambitions for the continued development of motorsport and mobility in Azerbaijan.    “The success of Formula 1 in Baku demonstrates what can be achieved through long-term commitment, strong organisation and a clear vision for the role that major sporting events can play in bringing people together and showcasing a country to the world. My congratulations on a fantastic ten years of racing and I look forward to many more.    “Our discussions also extended beyond motorsport. As the global federation for mobility organisations, the FIA is committed to working with governments and our Member Clubs such as the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation to make mobility safer, more accessible and more sustainable. I look forward to continuing our collaboration with our partners in Azerbaijan across these important areas.”   President Ben Sulayem’s visit comes as the FIA continues to strengthen its engagement across the region through its global network of Member Clubs and partners, including the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation and its President Anar Alakbarov.  The FIA has placed significant emphasis on growing motorsport participation and strengthening the pathway from grassroots competition to the highest levels of the sport, while using its global mobility network to advance road safety, sustainable mobility and accessibility. Azerbaijan’s position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, alongside continued investment in transport and infrastructure, provides opportunities for further collaboration across both pillars of the FIA’s work.  The meeting formed part of President Ben Sulayem’s programme in Azerbaijan, bringing together government, motorsport and mobility stakeholders to discuss opportunities to further develop the FIA’s activities in the country and wider region.        ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.  Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including seven FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all. title: F1 - 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix Post-Race Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  DRIVERS    1 – George RUSSELL (Mercedes)   2 – Max VERSTAPPEN (Red Bull Racing)   3 – Isack HADJAR (Red Bull Racing)       TRACK INTERVIEWS     (Conducted by Timo Glock)        Q: George, we see that big smile back on your face. That tells it all. I mean, it looked like an easy Saturday drive through Baku, but it got really spicy at the end. Talk us through those last laps.    George RUSSELL:  Yeah, I mean, it was amazing to be back on the top step of the podium. So, I do want to say a big thanks to my team because, you know, they’ve continued to believe in me through a tough moment, helped me come through it. I’m really proud to have had this weekend. And then, yeah, the first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing, getting a gap. Safety Car restart, especially when I saw Max behind, I thought, you know, it’s not going to be easy. And he drove incredibly at the end of the race. And then when the yellow flag came out, I lifted off the power and when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power. Max almost got me at the line. So, yeah, that would have been a real shame. But all in all, incredible weekend.      Q: But what is it? I mean, it looked like you came in this weekend, from lap one on, you had this confidence back. What changed in getting that performance out of the car?    GR:  I think it’s just having more experience with this sort of new driving style I’ve adopted. And every race since the break, I feel like I’ve gone from strength to strength and I feel like more myself again. So that’s really great.      Q: Well, Max, what a drive again, from P8 to P2, you came less than two tenths short, but how satisfying is that, to be back on the podium and having the chance of putting George under pressure?    Max VERSTAPPEN:  Yeah, we had a good race. I mean, the first stint was probably a little bit difficult with the Medium tyre, but we still worked our way into P3 and then we had a good restart, into P2. Then it was just like, 1 second, 1.1s. Then on the final lap, with the yellow flag, I think, George lost a bit of boost out of one corner and that’s why I caught up quite a bit and then to the line, I got close, but it was not enough.      Q: But Max, you threw everything at it. I mean, you brushed the walls a couple of times. I mean, that last wall, was that a sketchy one or was it sort of still under control?    MV:  It was okay. I just tried to open the corner probably a little bit too much, but the tyres were fine.      Q: Isack, I mean, what a comeback. Six weeks off, being on the podium. I mean, how happy are you coming back with a podium and a double podium for Red Bull?    Isack HADJAR:  Yeah, I’m happy. You know, it’s been very long, six weeks. You know, it’s been like six weeks since I enjoyed myself and now, I think it was the right time to come back. I felt strong and, you know, this weekend I really took it step by step. It’s a track you can end up in the wall really quickly. I didn’t need that to gain the confidence, so it was a very slow build-up, but it brought me here. So, I’m very, very happy for an actual first proper podium on pure pace. So I’m very, very delighted.      Q: And that tells you as well, like, the wrist is okay after doing a whole race distance. This is something different. Must be happy now to continue the rest of the season?    IH:  Yeah, now I’m completely satisfied. Even though it’s a bit numb, I’m happy. So, yeah, I’m really looking forward to get racing. It’s going to be a very packed schedule, so, yeah, I can’t wait to be in Sepang.      Q: Good. Thanks, Isack. George, coming back quickly again, you closed the gap by 15 points here. It’s going to be intense weeks ahead. What is the game plan of George Russell now in that championship?    GR:  Win every race. I mean, that’s the game plan. You know, my team-mate’s had an incredible season. He’s been pretty flawless throughout, but now we’re getting to crunch time. But I’m just going to focus on myself. You know, if I continue delivering performances like I’ve done this weekend, no matter what happens towards the end of the season, I’ll be happy because it’s been a real tough period for me but I feel like I’ve come through the other side.      PRESS CONFERENCE        Q: George, what a weekend for you. Pole position yesterday by eight tenths, then victory today by one tenth. But just tell us what it all means to you.    GR:  Yeah, it feels great, to be honest. I’m very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year because there’s been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges, to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better. And F1 is so tough, you don’t get opportunities to practice this, and finally it’s coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once did, and I’m gaining confidence. And especially on circuits like this, it just allows you to eke out that little bit more on the brakes, get that little bit closer to the walls, and it’s been a flawless weekend.      Q: You’re gaining confidence. Do you feel rejuvenated?    GR:  I think I never lost that faith in myself, even through a tough moments I knew there was a reason why I was off the pace. It wasn’t like I just suddenly forgot how to drive, and I knew I would be able to find it again. I just had to be patient. So, I feel confident. You know, it’s been four races since the break. I’ve been on the front row in three of them, three podiums from the four races. I feel I can fight for victory week-in, week-out now.      Q: Let’s break down the race. It was definitely one of two halves. You looked serene out front in the first stint. Were you happier on the Medium tyre?    GR:  Well, I think Max and myself were probably the two quickest drivers out there, and the soft tyre looked the best tyre, so I think that was maybe not allowing Max to get past Piastri. But, yeah, clearly that final stint, the two of us were exceptionally fast and, you know, we were pulling a second a lap almost to the rest of the field, which was really good fun, to be honest. It felt like qualifying laps, one after another, and I knew I couldn’t make a single mistake. But certainly, the last 10 laps were a bit more tense than the first 40.      Q: Talk us through the Safety Car restarts. Did they play out as you’d hoped?    GR:  Yeah, I mean, it’s the first restart I’ve done this season from the lead. These power units are very challenging at restarts, getting the battery in the right place for turbo spinning at the right speed, and I always do good preparation on what I want to do at a restart. It needs a lot more thought into it than ever before. But, you know, I was keeping an eye on my mirrors where Max was, and I had waited for that moment when the gap was just slightly larger and managed to break him because I knew if he saw half a chance, he would have been sending it down the inside. So, I was pleased with it.      Q: You’re happy with the car here, you’re happy with your performance. Are you confident that it’ll be the same next weekend at a permanent racetrack like Sepang?    GR:  I’m really excited. We’ve got the upgrades coming soon. That’s going to be a good step forward. Our car has been working exceptionally well on the low-drag circuits. We’ve got a really efficient car, so here at Monza we’ve been exceptionally fast. But I think from next week onwards, we’re hoping to make a bigger step to the rest of the field. But nothing’s sure until we see how it pans out in reality.      Q: Alright, very well done. Thank you very much for that, George. Max, let’s come to you. Great race by you, very well done. Given how close you were at the line, does today feel like a “what if” race for you? What if you’d started a little bit higher up the grid?    MV:  Yeah, I mean, we should have done that, right? I mean, that’s what happened yesterday. You know, you have a problem and then that means that you have to start P8. But I think even if I started second, I think the pace of George, it would have been very hard to pass. So maybe I could have followed him a bit better, of course, then in that first stint. Then you box, you’re second, behind, and then probably we would have done the same race, just pushing each other along. It would have for sure made my first stint a bit easier instead of overtaking all the cars that I had to. But, yeah, for sure the Soft tyre was much better than the Medium because I just had the first few laps in the first stint were very strong, but then, yeah, the tyres were just not working and it was quite a bit of, like, just surviving in the first stint, trying to go as long as possible. And then the Safety Car actually came at the right time to swap to the Soft tyres. And then I have to say that, yeah, those last laps were very enjoyable because there was barely any deg, really. We were just pushing to the end and the gap was always, like, one second, 1.1, so that was nice. And, of course, it looked close on the line, but I think that was more because I think George suffered from a little bit of boost lag in 15 with the yellow flag. So if you look at the last stint, it was always one second, so that’s probably also where we would have finished.      Q: How much of a boost is the performance of the car here with the upgrades, both for you and the whole team?    MV:  Yeah, it was good. I mean, the car was feeling very good all weekend. Okay, then we had the issue in qualifying with the engine. We still, of course, have some limitations with the car that I’ve mentioned many times that probably are not fixable for this year. So we know that for next year that needs a lot of work. But the balance in the car was strong. But like George said, for Malaysia, if they’re bringing an upgrade, it’s going to look a little bit more difficult for us.      Q: This was podium number seven for you this year. Are there any tracks that you’re particularly looking forward to coming up where you think you can be this competitive again?    MV:  We don’t know. I mean, if Mercedes is bringing an upgrade and it works, then they take a step ahead, and that’s not what you want. It will make it even more difficult to win, but we’ll try every single weekend and, of course, if the opportunity is there, we go for it.      Q: Max, very well done to you. Thank you for that. Isack, let’s come to you. What a comeback. Your second podium of the season after six weeks out. Just how sweet does this moment feel for you?    IH:  Yeah, I must say I came back at the right time in terms of an injury point of view and, at the same time, in terms of what the car is capable of. You know, the way I left the car in Budapest, I was not really satisfied, and coming back after a couple of races, definitely made a step. So, yeah, definitely happy about that. And, you know, in terms of the approach, I took it really slowly, the whole weekend, because it’s a demanding track to come back to. I don’t want to be in the wall. And, yeah, like I said, it’s a tough track to come back to. The approach was great. It brought me to that P3. So, yeah, I can’t really do much better than that.      Q: As you say, it’s a tough track. Any issues at all with the wrist?    IH:  No.      Q: And then when you look at the weekend as a whole, just how much have you missed racing over these last six weeks?    IH:  Yeah, it’s been a moment now. I felt like I had, like, a whole winter break, which is not really what you want in the middle of the season. So, yeah, I definitely missed it. You know, the adrenaline, those Q3 laps, the restart, and, yeah, it’s good to be back fighting with the other drivers. It’s what I love to do. So hopefully I use a bit more my brain when I go boxing next time.      Q: There was some radio chat about vibrations in the gearbox while you were behind the Safety Car. Did that clear up once the race went green?    IH:  No, it was quite noisy and I felt a lot of vibrations. I was a bit stressed, to be honest. I wasn’t really sure, but everything was fine until the very end. But, yeah, let’s see if it’s just some irrelevant noise or actually relevant. Let’s see.      Q: Okay. Look, final one. Just how much confidence does this weekend as a whole give you going to Sepang next weekend?    IH:  Yeah, a lot. You know, in the end, the Monaco podium, of course it was a podium, but it was not on pure pace, not because I qualified in the top three or whatever. You know, I felt like this is my first time with the team that I actually get to do a very clean weekend and actually, like, fight my way into that podium. So actually, for me, it feels like a real first and, yeah, it gives me good confidence heading into the next races.     QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR      Q: (Frédéric Ferret – L’Equipe) Question to George Russell. What does the Grand Slam mean for you? Question for Max: what does the podium of Isack mean for the team and how do you rate him? And question for Isack: you have the Zandvoort trophy on your helmet. Do you plan to make the same helmet next week?    GR:  Yeah, I think it’s probably my first Grand Slam in Formula 1 and, for sure, the most dominant weekend I’ve had in my career. So that has come at a really great moment. And also to achieve it on a circuit that requires so much commitment and confidence, I’m really proud of because I think it would have been very easy for me to lose the faith this season. Not necessarily about winning the championship, but in terms of my ability, and that never happened.   MV:  Yeah, well, this is what the team wants, to have the two cars on the podium when possible. So, maximising the result, and I think we did that today. So that’s very good. And, yeah, for sure, I mean, it’s working really well with Isack in the team and we just need to keep that going.      Q: How do you rate him, just to follow up?    MV:  Yeah, like, it’s working really well within the team, you know. So, of course, I mean, if you’re on the podium together, then I think you’re doing a good job.   IH:  I mean, it was pure coincidence. I should have raced that helmet in Zandvoort. I made it, so I wanted to, even though I skipped those races, wear it for that occasion. But now it’s a retired helmet and has a podium, so it’s good.      Q: (Leonid Kliuev – GrandePremio.com) Question for all three. Behind you, Franco was out of control into Turn 1 at the restart. Several people were taken out. Franco apologised. Lando said that, and I’m paraphrasing, he didn’t see the replay, but whoever is taking people out in this fashion should have a race ban, and he emphasised the race ban. Is that perhaps too harsh for your liking?     GR:  Yeah, I think that’s too harsh, personally. I think Safety Car restarts, cold tyres, a very small mistake can have big consequences. And from what I saw today, that’s what it looked like. It was a small error that had a big consequence. I think, personally, race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless. So I think it was unfortunate.   MV:  Yeah, I think as long, of course, the driver that caused it is aware of what he did, right, and apologised. And, I mean, yeah, that happens. I mean, like, a small mistake or misjudgement, you lock up, it’s on the inside, low grip, and, of course, then I guess a bit unfortunate that it involves so many cars. But, yeah, unfortunate, happens, and it’s not nice, I think. Not nice for anyone involved, right? But like George said, I think, yeah, a race ban probably is a bit much.   IH:  From   my side, I think the track is not good enough. You move out of the racing line, it starts to be very bumpy. It’s hard to generate temperature behind the Safety Car, it’s going quite slowly. So then, yeah, you just overdo it and then it has big, big consequences. So, I think, yeah, a race ban is way too harsh.      Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) It’s a question to both Red Bull drivers. Has your feeling behind the wheel, the feeling in the car, changed at all with this upgrade? So, do you feel more confident to attack the corners now, or is it simply quicker but still with the same issues?    IH:  Yeah, to be honest, Baku is a very specific track, specific tarmac. But like I said, to me, the way the car was behaving in terms of through-corner balance this weekend, from lap one in FP1, I was like, “Okay, this is looking pretty good.” Then the second half of the car, we’re lacking compared to Mercedes, definitely. But, you know, in terms of handling on the brakes, the car was, to me, compared to Budapest, it definitely did a step. So, yeah, I’m really pleased with that.   MV:  Yeah, I mean, it’s a unique track. It’s, like, mainly 90-degree corners. But, yeah, it felt probably a little bit more together balance-wise. But like I said, we have other issues in the car that we really need to fix because there is also just free lap time in that, and that’s what we are working on. But the performance items, they worked well and we’ve been fairly happy all weekend, really, with what I had from the car.      Q: (Phil Duncan – PA) George, after the race you spoke about your plan now is to go and win every race. It’s the crunch part of the season. You obviously don’t have the target on your back that Kimi does. Do you think that you can use that to your advantage, that you’re chasing and that you can help apply the pressure that way?    GR:  Yeah, for sure. There’s much less pressure on me than there is him. As I said yesterday, he’s had an incredibly flawless season. Yesterday was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session, qualifying, race, and he still came home in P5 today. I didn’t really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn’t strong enough. Now I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, you know, I feel very much I would have been able to fight. Now I’ve got this big deficit. It can change quick. So I’m not chasing that. I’m chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be.      Q: (Sergey Podosenov – News.ru) As we have seen today, Baku City Circuit proved its unpredictable nature. How did the unique challenges of racing in Azerbaijan today impact your strategy and mindset on the way to the podium? Thank you.     GR:  Yeah, well, I must say Max and I spoke about this. The final stint, I think, is the most amount of fun I’ve had in a race for as long as I can remember because the tyre felt great. We were pushing flat out every single lap. It was like qualifying one after another. You needed to be so alert around this circuit because the walls are so close, especially through the castle. You’re threading the needle. But, yeah, those final 10 laps felt really, really fun. And it almost felt like the stories I hear of the drivers in the early-mid 2000s, of when every lap was like a qualifying lap. The heart rate is higher, you’re pushing the limit every single lap, there’s no management. We’ve had a lot of conversations this year about PU energy management, but the tyre management is still there and it has been there for years and years. But just with how the temperatures and the circuit fell out today, with the tyres there was no management, and that was exceptionally fun.   MV:  Yeah, exactly that. I mean, last stint was fun. Kissed a few walls as well, just to leave my mark here in Baku. So, yeah, it’s always very challenging around here, qualifying and in the race now at the end as well, just pushing flat out. Comes, of course, with risk, being close to certain walls on the inside, the outside. But it’s cool.      ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 6:47pm  Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 6:47pm

title: F1 – Russell holds off Verstappen to win dramatic Azerbaijan Grand Prix as Red Bull claim double podium
summary: Sport news George Russell secured his third victory of the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship season with a hard-fought win in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, holding off Max Verstappen by just 0.196 seconds after a late-race battle around the Baku City Circuit.  The Mercedes driver converted pole position into victory despite two closely linked Safety Car periods that closed up the field. Verstappen finished second for Red Bull Racing, while team-mate Isack Hadjar completed the podium in third on his return from injury. Charles Leclerc finished fourth for Ferrari, ahead of Kimi Antonelli, who recovered from 16th on the grid to take fifth.  Lewis Hamilton was sixth, followed by Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad and the Haas pair of Esteban Ocon and Oliver Bearman. Carlos Sainz completed the top 10 for Williams, while Oscar Piastri dropped from the leading group to 14th after a late error.  The race also saw six drivers fail to finish, including McLaren’s Lando Norris, who was caught up in a Turn 1 incident involving Alpine team-mates Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly.  At the start, Russell made a clean getaway from pole and immediately established control of the race. Piastri moved into second ahead of Leclerc, while Norris passed Hadjar to take fourth. Verstappen also made progress, moving ahead of Gasly and Hamilton before setting his sights on the cars immediately ahead.  Russell quickly opened a gap at the front, while Piastri came under pressure from the two Red Bulls. Hadjar reclaimed fourth from Norris before Verstappen followed through, and the Red Bull pair then began to close on Leclerc.  Hadjar then attacked Leclerc around the outside at Turn 1 before completing the pass in turn 3. Verstappen soon followed him past the Ferrari, leaving the Red Bulls in close pursuit of Piastri.  The long run towards Turn 1 proved particularly important. The Red Bulls appeared to have an advantage on the straights, while Piastri’s McLaren struggled for traction exiting Turn 16. Verstappen eventually moved ahead of Hadjar and began to pressure Piastri for second.  The battle behind the leaders remained close, with Antonelli gradually recovering from his difficult opening lap. The Mercedes driver had dropped to 17th but began working his way forward, picking off a succession of cars as the race developed.  At the front, Russell continued to extend his advantage, reaching almost 10 seconds over Piastri by the halfway stage. Yet the Mercedes driver was not entirely comfortable, brushing the wall at Turn 15 and reporting concerns about his tyre pressure.  Norris was also struggling to make progress. After locking up at Turn 5 and running deep, he lost places to Hamilton and Gasly before another mistake on the start/finish straight dropped him further back.  The first major interruption came on Lap 30, when Alexander Albon locked up at Turn 6 while battling Haas’ Esteban Ocon. The Williams driver hit the barriers and brought out the Safety Car.  With the leading drivers yet to make their scheduled pit stops, the neutralisation provided an opportunity to change tyres without losing significant track position. Russell retained the lead, while Red Bull executed a double stack that kept Verstappen and Hadjar together behind Piastri.  The restart produced another decisive sequence of events. Verstappen finally moved past Piastri for second, while further back Colapinto locked up approaching Turn 1 and collided with his Alpine team-mate Gasly. Gasly was then unable to avoid Norris, with all three cars leaving the circuit and retiring from the race.  The incident triggered a second Safety Car and dramatically altered the complexion of the Grand Prix.  Russell again led Verstappen at the restart, with Piastri third and Hadjar fourth. Leclerc and Hamilton followed, while Antonelli had moved into contention after benefiting from the earlier incidents.  But the race remained unforgiving. Piastri, under pressure from Hadjar, locked up into Turn 1 on the following lap and spun, dropping from a potential podium position to the rear of the field. The McLaren driver eventually recovered to 14th at the finish.  Antonelli continued his recovery and passed Hamilton with eight laps remaining to move into fifth. The Italian’s progress represented a remarkable recovery from his qualifying accident and 16th-place starting position.  At the front, however, all attention was now focused on Russell and Verstappen. The Mercedes driver had appeared to have the race under control before the Safety Cars, but the two interruptions had brought Verstappen back into contention. The Red Bull remained within a few tenths through the closing laps, applying sustained pressure as Russell negotiated the narrow streets of Baku.  A late yellow flag was caused by Valtteri Bottas, who put his Cadillac into the barriers, but the incident did not prevent the leaders from continuing their battle. As the 51st and final lap began, Verstappen remained close enough to attack. He drew alongside Russell on the run towards the finish, creating a final drag race along the start/finish straight.  Russell held his line and maintained enough momentum to keep the Red Bull behind him, crossing the finish line just 0.196 seconds ahead of Verstappen to claim his eighth career Formula 1 victory.  Hadjar completed a double podium for Red Bull in third, 10.704 seconds behind the winner, while Leclerc finished fourth. Antonelli’s recovery was completed with fifth place, 14.512 seconds from Russell, with Hamilton sixth.  Lindblad took seventh for Racing Bulls, although his result was subject to investigation following his earlier contact with team-mate Liam Lawson. Ocon and Bearman gave Haas a double points finish in eighth and ninth, while Sainz claimed the final point-paying position in 10th.   2026 FIA Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix – Race  1 George Russell Mercedes 51 -  2 Max Verstappen Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 51 0.196 3 Isack Hadjar Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 51 10.704 4 Charles Leclerc Ferrari 51 14.136 5 Kimi Antonelli Mercedes 51 14.512 6 Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 51 22.382 7 Arvid Lindblad Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 51 31.159 8 Esteban Ocon Haas/Ferrari 51 31.189 9 Oliver Bearman Haas/Ferrari 51 31.929 10 Carlos Sainz Williams/Mercedes 51 32.416 11 Nico Hülkenberg Audi 51 33.231 12 Liam Lawson Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 51 34.013 13 Gabriel Bortoleto Audi 51 34.230 14 Oscar Piastri McLaren/Mercedes 51 36.401 15 Sergio Pérez Cadillac/Ferrari 51 41.400 16 Valtteri Bottas Cadillac/Ferrari 49 - 2 laps      Franco Colapinto Alpine/Mercedes 36 – Retirement      Lando Norris McLaren/Mercedes 35 – Retirement      Pierre Gasly Alpine/Mercedes 35 – Retirement      Alexander Albon Williams/Mercedes 29 – Retirement      Fernando Alonso Aston Martin/Honda 20 – Retirement      Lance Stroll Aston Martin/Honda 7 - Retirement       FIA Formula One World Championship    F1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026F101 Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 5:35pm  Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 5:35pm

title: WEC: Alpine on pole at Fuji after rain leads to qualifying cancellation
summary: Sport news Heavy rain swept across Fuji Speedway ahead of the scheduled start of the LMGT3 qualifying session, which began on time but was red-flagged after François Heriau went off in his #21 VISTA AF Corse Ferrari.  The decision was then taken to cancel the remaining qualifying sessions due to the forecast of heavier rain and fog at Fuji Speedway.  That meant that, in accordance with the regulations, the grid was set according to the best times from the three Free Practice sessions held across Friday and Saturday morning.  Victor Martins’ FP2 time of 1m40.594s ensured that the #36 Alpine will start from pole position, marking the first-ever WEC pole for the A424 Hypercar.  It was a double celebration for the French manufacturer as the #35 car will join its sister Hypercar on the front row, putting Alpine in a strong position to defend last year’s victory at the venue.  Second on the grid should initially have been the #007 Aston Martin Valkyrie, but it was demoted to fourth after receiving a penalty for causing a collision in the morning’s FP3 session.  Starting third on the grid will be the #17 Genesis Magma Hypercar, meaning the Korean manufacturer will begin tomorrow’s race from by far its best-ever starting position.  In the LMGT3 category, the #77 Proton Competition Ford Mustang will start from pole position after setting the fastest FP2 time on Friday afternoon. It marks the first pole position for a Ford Mustang since the Lone Star Le Mans race at COTA in September 2025.       WEC  Endurance  6 Hours of Fuji  WEC   Sport 1SportWECWECEndurance6 Hours of Fuji00 Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 9:08am  Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 9:08am

title: ICA Statement regarding ICA Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09
summary: Sport news The FIA Courts are aware of public comments questioning the independence and impartiality of the judges of the panel that decided Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09.  The FIA Courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration.  All judges are elected by the FIA General Assemblies, some of them upon proposition of a group of at least five F1 teams in accordance with the FIA Statutes. They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA Compliance Officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties.  At both the beginning and conclusion of the hearing, the parties were invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the Court. None did so. No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the Court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.  The ICA emphasizes the importance of constituting panels with judges from different cultural and geographical backgrounds. This helps ensure that the deliberations and discussions reflect a diversity of legal traditions, perspectives and approaches, further strengthening the fairness, independence, credibility of the process and access to a fair trial.  A Court’s decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges. The Court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges. The FIA Courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process.      Laurent Anselmi (President of the ICA and of the FIA Judges Congress), Rui Botica Santos (President of the IT and Vice-President of the Judges Congress), Waltraud Wünsch (Vice-President of the ICA) and Gérard Martin (Vice-President of the IT). title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem Meets Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to Discuss Shared Motorsport Priorities
summary: FIA news Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, met with Lebanese President His Excellency Joseph Aoun today after attending the Rally of Lebanon, an event he won four times in a distinguished rally driving career which established him as a sporting ambassador for the Arab world.  The meeting at Baabda Palace provided an opportunity to reflect on the continued success of the event, and Lebanon’s position as a rallying stronghold in the Middle East.  Ben Sulayem accepted an official invitation from the Automobile and Touring Club of Lebanon and President Nabil ‘Billy’ Karam to attend the 48th Rally of Lebanon. The fourth round of this year’s FIA Middle East Rally Championship reached its finish at the ATCL in Kaslik, Jounieh last night (Sunday) with victory going to Lebanon’s Roger Feghali and co-driver Joseph Matar.   “I was pleased to meet with President Aoun and discuss our shared priorities for the future of motorsport,”   said FIA President Ben Sulayem.   “The Rally of Lebanon provided me with many great memories during my rally driving career, and I’m thrilled to once again experience the excitement this event creates for competitors and the country’s passionate motor sport fans.”    “The event has a rich history embedded in the origins of Middle East motorsport. It is firmly established as the home for asphalt rallying in the region, and plays a key role in our plans to ensure the long-term future of the FIA Middle East Rally Championship.    “Lebanon has always felt like a special place for me, and I want to thank the ATCL and its President, Nabil Karam, for their warm welcome and hospitality. I’m delighted to have met up again with some of the friends I have made at the club, and across the country over the years.”   Ben Sulayem’s legendary rally-driving achievements brought him widespread recognition, and he was awarded the President’s Cup by Lebanese President Amine Gemayel in 1987, and the Medal of Honour from Lebanese President Emile Lahoud in 1999.  Each of his four victories in the Rally of Lebanon, in 1987, 1991, 1998 and 1999, helped him secure the FIA Middle East Rally Championship title, which he won 14 times overall. He achieved the last three of those victories alongside his long-time co-driver Ronan Morgan.  Beyond his success in Middle East rallying, Ben Sulayem recorded his first overseas win in Turkey in 1991, and secured World Rally Championship Group N victories in Spain and Argentina over the following two years. He retired from competitive rallying in 2002.  In July, the FIA announced a landmark long-term commercial rights agreement for the FIA WRC and FIA European Rally Championship, following the acquisition of WRC Promoter GmbH by Cosmobilis and Park Square Capital. Designed to bring significant new investment into the sport, the biggest deal in the history of these championships supported the FIA’s vision under President Ben Sulayem, who said at the time:  “Rallying is a huge part of my personal story. It has shaped who I am and how I work, and I am deeply committed to its future.”       ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.  Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including seven FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.
